original_question: Determine whether the Diophantine equation x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2 has infinitely many integer solutions that are not permutations of (x, y, z) = (1 - 6t^3, -6t^2, 1 + 6t^3) for integers t.
target_in_paper: Section 2 of the paper, in the part on existence of polynomial parametrizations: the open problem is about classifying nonconstant polynomial parametrizations of x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2 and asking whether any essentially different parametrization exists beyond the standard one.
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the correct Diophantine equation and the standard known one-parameter family (up to harmless sign/order conventions). It also correctly aims at the distinction between the known family and possible additional families.
missing_details: The paper-faithful problem is about polynomial parametrizations, not about isolated integer solutions.
The ambient ring should be Q[t] (polynomials in one variable with rational coefficients), not merely Z.
The unknowns should be polynomial triples (x(t), y(t), z(t)) satisfying the identity x(t)^3 + y(t)^3 + z(t)^3 = 2 identically in t.
The relevant solutions are nonconstant polynomial triples; otherwise constant solutions trivially exist.
Equivalence is not just permutation of the displayed triple: one also identifies parametrizations obtained by substituting t = u(t) with u(t) in Q[t].

Because there are already known integer solutions to x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2 outside the displayed family, asking for infinitely many integer solutions outside that family does not match the paper's actual intent.

To be stand-alone, the question should state explicitly that the standard family is (1 + 6u(t)^3, 1 - 6u(t)^3, -6u(t)^2), up to permutation; your displayed variant is an equivalent reordered/sign-changed version.
The paper's focus here is whether there exist any essentially different nonconstant polynomial families, not whether there are infinitely many exceptional integer points.
refined_question: Do there exist any nonconstant polynomial triples x(t), y(t), z(t) in Q[t] satisfying the identity x(t)^3 + y(t)^3 + z(t)^3 = 2 that are not obtained, up to permutation of the three coordinates, from the standard family (1 + 6u(t)^3, 1 - 6u(t)^3, -6u(t)^2) for some polynomial u(t) in Q[t]?
justification: The draft is aimed at the right equation and the right known family, but it shifts the target from polynomial parametrizations to integer points. In the surrounding context used by the paper, the open issue for x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2 is the existence of any essentially new nonconstant polynomial parametrization over Q, beyond the standard family and its obvious reparametrizations/permutations. That is the sharp stand-alone formulation closest to the paper's intent. The stronger-looking question about infinitely many exceptional integer triples is not the same problem, and in fact isolated integer triples outside the standard family are already known in the literature cited around this problem.
